slides.title: Riemannian Connections
slides.notes: Open by positioning the metric as the new ingredient that removes ambiguity from the connection story. Chapter 3 allowed many affine and linear connections; this chapter asks what happens when lengths, angles, and distance must be preserved by parallel transport.

slides.title: Route Through The Source Span
slides.notes: Use this map to keep the lecture from scattering across the many propositions. The conceptual sequence is metric, distinguished connection, distance geometry, completeness, and holonomy splitting. Each later theorem is a stronger way of saying that the metric controls both local and global motion.

slides.title: Riemannian Metrics As Moving Inner Products
slides.notes: Make the metric concrete before discussing connections. Students should see the metric as a smoothly varying ruler on tangent spaces, not merely as a matrix. The coordinate matrix is useful, but the invariant object is the inner product and the geometric measurements it supports.

slides.title: Length And Distance Enter The Story
slides.notes: Present distance as the first global object built from the metric. At this stage it is defined by an infimum, so it is not yet obvious that geodesics realize it or that it gives the manifold topology. The normal-coordinate section supplies the local proof mechanism.

slides.title: The Levi-Civita Connection
slides.notes: This is the chapter's central selection theorem. The previous chapter made connections flexible; the metric imposes two geometric demands that determine one connection. Explain metric compatibility as preserving measuring devices, and torsion-free behavior as aligning infinitesimal parallelograms with the bracket structure.

slides.title: Koszul Formula As A Recipe
slides.notes: Do not ask students to memorize the full displayed identity as a first move. The important idea is that the metric lets one solve for the unknown covariant derivative by testing it against every vector field. The bracket corrections are exactly the price of non-coordinate motion.

slides.title: Christoffel Symbols From The Metric
slides.notes: This is where the abstract uniqueness theorem becomes a calculational tool. The metric coefficients and their first derivatives determine the Christoffel symbols. Emphasize the standard warning: symbols help compute geodesics and curvature, but the symbols themselves depend on the chosen coordinates.

slides.title: Isometries Commute With Riemannian Transport
slides.notes: This slide is a good place to show the power of uniqueness. Instead of computing transported vectors directly, pull the connection through an isometry and notice that the two defining properties survive. The conclusion automatically carries geodesics, parallel transport, and holonomy information across the map.

slides.title: Normal Coordinates Spend Geodesics As Coordinates
slides.notes: Normal coordinates should feel like a controlled laboratory rather than a trick. The exponential map converts a small tangent ball into a neighborhood of the manifold, and straight radial lines become geodesics. This gives local access to distance, spheres, and minimizing behavior.

slides.title: Convex Neighborhoods Localize Minimizing Geometry
slides.notes: Convex neighborhoods are the local control device for the rest of the chapter. They certify uniqueness and minimizing behavior without assuming global completeness. Stress that the theorem is not saying all geodesics minimize forever, only that sufficiently small regions have reliable geodesic coordinates.

slides.title: Distance Remembers The Riemannian Metric
slides.notes: This theorem is a conceptual checkpoint: the distance function is not an external decoration but a complete carrier of the Riemannian metric. Convex neighborhoods and normal coordinates let one turn preservation of distances into preservation of geodesics and then into preservation of inner products.

slides.title: Completeness: Four Faces Of The Same Condition
slides.notes: Treat completeness as the moment local geodesic control becomes global. The theorem ties together four languages: ordinary metric spaces, geodesic differential equations, compactness of balls, and development in tangent space. The existence of minimizing geodesics between any two points is the visible payoff.

slides.title: Riemannian Holonomy Is Orthogonal
slides.notes: Bring holonomy back as the memory of parallel transport around loops. Because the Levi-Civita connection preserves the metric, the holonomy group acts by orthogonal transformations. Reducibility is therefore a metric statement about invariant orthogonal subspaces in a single tangent space.

slides.title: Parallel Distributions Create Local Products
slides.notes: This is the local bridge from representation theory to geometry. A holonomy-invariant subspace is not just algebra at one point; parallel transport spreads it into a distribution. Orthogonality gives a partner distribution, and the torsion-free metric connection makes the corresponding leaves behave like product factors.

slides.title: The de Rham Decomposition Theorem
slides.notes: State the theorem as the global payoff of the holonomy discussion. Completeness and simple connectedness are the hypotheses that let local product geometry integrate without monodromy. The Euclidean factor records directions fixed by holonomy, while the other factors are irreducible pieces.

slides.title: Affine Holonomy Adds Translations
slides.notes: Affine holonomy extends the linear picture by allowing translations of the affine tangent space. The chapter's dichotomy says that irreducibility leaves little room: either translations fill the tangent space, or a fixed point collapses the geometry toward the Euclidean case under completeness and simple connectedness.

slides.title: Notebook Lab: Turn The Chapter Into Checks
slides.notes: Tie the lecture back to the notebook's deliberately small computational artifacts. The goal is not to reproduce the textbook but to create inspection habits: identify the metric data, test a local model, and decide which invariant changes when an assumption is perturbed or removed.

slides.title: Closing Checklist
slides.notes: Close by giving students a compact reading protocol. For any Riemannian connection question, ask what the metric measures, what the Levi-Civita connection transports, whether geodesics minimize locally or globally, and how holonomy acts on tangent directions. That checklist prepares the curvature chapter.
